What the River Keeps: Memory as Inheritance in Beloved

Toni Morrison's Beloved treats memory less as a record than as a debt that every character inherits whether or not they consent to it. The river and the clearing, the novel's two great gathering places, are where that debt comes due. Sethe calls the past "rememory," a word that refuses the comfort of the past tense. What she remembers is not hers alone; it waits for whoever walks into it, and it does not ask permission. (Morrison 35) Critics have often read the clearing as a site of healing, the place where Baby Suggs asks her congregation to love their flesh. Yet the clearing also works as a ledger, recording what the community owes and what it refuses to pay.

James Baldwin's claim that history is "the price of the ticket" helps explain why the novel will not let anyone receive grace without first paying for it. The community that gathers there is also the community that later refuses to warn Sethe, and the novel insists that both gestures belong to the same place. The river, by contrast, is where the dead cross back. Beloved arrives from the water fully dressed, as if the current had kept her waiting, and the townspeople's silence is the condition of her return. Paul D carries his own memories in a tobacco tin where his heart used to be, rusted shut against everything Sweet Home took from him.

Denver, who was born in a boat on the Ohio, learns that the house at 124 Bluestone Road is less a home than an archive with a temper. Each of these figures discovers that forgetting is not an option the novel offers, only a postponement it occasionally tolerates. The structure of the book enforces the same lesson, circling back to scenes it has already described and adding a detail each time.

Readers are made to experience memory as Sethe does, in fragments that refuse to stay where they were put. Morrison once described her task as filling in the blanks that the slave narratives left, the interior lives that their authors could not afford to record. That task requires a form in which the past is never quite past, and in which every present scene is crowded by the ones behind it. The novel's final pages repeat the phrase "It was not a story to pass on" until its meaning splits in two. It was not a story to hand down, and it was not a story to pass by; the ambiguity is the inheritance. To read Beloved closely is to accept that obligation, and to notice how often the novel asks its readers to stay in the clearing a little longer.

Stamp Paid's ribbon, the red cardinal feather in a dead girl's hair, becomes another entry in a ledger no one asked to keep. The house itself seems to participate in the accounting, rattling its furniture whenever someone tries to close the books too early.
